## Introduction

In this five-minute demonstration, we will work out what a reader
should cite to find the materials for a particular analysis. We will
use a prepared Zenodo record and inspect its metadata together.

A Git commit identifies a repository revision. A GitHub release gives
a tagged revision a name and a place for release notes and assets.
Zenodo can archive a copy of selected files and issue a DOI. An
archive makes the cited files available under the access conditions
of that record.
[Zenodo records and DOIs](https://help.zenodo.org/docs/deposit/describe-records/reserve-doi/)

## Inspect a record

Open the workshop's archived `v0.2.0` release. Find the creators,
access conditions, and the ZIP of that revision. Compare the Zenodo
version DOI with the GitHub release tag and the concept DOI in
`CITATION.cff`. Cite the version DOI for the files supporting a
result. Cite the concept DOI when referring to the evolving project.
[Version archive](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24357028) ·
[Concept DOI](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24342489) ·
[GitHub release](https://github.com/JBris/open-and-reproducible-science-in-r/releases/tag/v0.2.0)

## Decide what to archive

For the `HealthWellbeing` analysis, assemble a candidate list:

-   The exact code revision, pipeline script, and Quarto report source.
-   The report and summary CSV, where upstream terms permit sharing.
-   The lockfile, actual environment record, and container digest if
    the run used a container.
-   The source citation, download URL, checksum, pin version and
    study inclusion rule, plus the relevant metadata and reuse terms.

The upstream download is publicly accessible. Confirm its reuse terms
before including the raw file, pinned copies, or derivatives in a
deposit. If you cannot include a copy, document how an authorised
reader can obtain the source and recreate the selected input. A pin
version identifies an object in a particular board. Preserving a
version identifier with the checksum and filter lets another reader
understand what that object contained.

## Try it yourself

Point to the DOI you would cite for the files you inspected.
Identify one item that would help a reader recreate the precise
version of the input. Explain how you would document its access
conditions. We will discuss the deposit together during the
demonstration.

## Checkpoint {#zenodo-checkpoint}

You can connect a cited archive to a specific version, distinguish
its DOI from a GitHub release tag, and list the files and metadata
a reader needs. Use the archive's own citation for the record you
inspected and cite the original review separately for the study data.

We will finish with optional extensions and discussion.
